title: He Ran Off With the Mathematician's Wife Who Helped Build Cubism. He Still Wouldn't Join It.
standfirst: In 1907 André Derain began an affair with the wife of Maurice Princet, the actuary whose talk of a fourth dimension shaped how Picasso and Braque built Cubism. Princet drifted out of the circle that made the movement; Derain, closer to its centre, spent years refusing to follow it in — and this undated village, catalogued as Cubism, was painted deep inside the alternative he built instead.

sections.heading: In 1907, He Began an Affair With the House Mathematician's Wife
sections.body: Derain met Alice Géry in Montmartre in the autumn of 1907. She was married at the time to Maurice Princet, a young actuary known to the painters at the Bateau-Lavoir as ["the mathematician of cubism"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Princet) for introducing them to Henri Poincaré's writing on the fourth dimension — he had put a 1903 treatise on four-dimensional geometry in front of Picasso himself, and Marcel Duchamp later admitted the group "weren't mathematicians at all, but we really did believe in Princet." Wikipedia's account of Princet is blunt about what happened next: "Princet's wife left him for André Derain, and he drifted away from the circle of artists at the Bateau-Lavoir." Alice and Derain eventually married in 1926. Cubism kept Picasso and Braque. It lost, in the same affair, the man who had been feeding it geometry.

sections.heading: Two Years Earlier, He Had Already Rewritten the Rules Once
sections.body: Derain did not need Princet's circle to matter. In the summer of 1905 he and Henri Matisse worked side by side in the Mediterranean fishing town of Collioure, pushing colour away from anything a landscape actually looked like. Shown that autumn at the Salon d'Automne, the pictures struck the critic Louis Vauxcelles as the work of wild animals, and "les Fauves" stuck as a name for the short, loud movement Derain had co-founded before he turned thirty.

sections.heading: By 1910 He Had Made Up His Mind About Cézanne and Cubism
sections.body: The dealer Ambroise Vollard sent Derain to London in 1906, and by 1907 Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler — soon to be Picasso's dealer too — had bought his entire studio output, pulling him into Montmartre alongside Picasso and Braque. For several years the three men shared an interest in Cézanne's structure and in African sculpture, the same raw material Cubism was built from. Then, around 1910, Derain walked back out of it, telling anyone listening that ["Cézanne disturbs me"](https://theartstory.org/artist/derain-andre/) because "his efforts to achieve perfection are incompatible with the liberty of human thought." He had spent three years at the centre of the group that invented Cubism and left before it had a name people agreed on.

sections.heading: His Own Answer Was Called the Gothic Period — and This Village Sits Inside It
sections.body: What Derain built in Cubism's place, from 1911 to 1914, is usually filed as his Gothic period: colour pulled back, forms simplified, the reference point no longer Picasso's studio but Romanesque sculpture and the early Italian masters. WikiArt dates this canvas to around 1912, oil on canvas, 65 by 81.5 centimetres, now in a private collection — squarely inside those Gothic years, and nowhere near the analytic fragmentation Picasso and Braque were refining in Paris that same season. The record behind this page still calls it Cubism anyway, the label for the exact circle Derain had just spent a year leaving.

sections.heading: By 1928 the Rebel Had Become the Establishment
sections.body: War service from 1914 to 1919 interrupted everything; afterward Derain designed sets for Diaghilev's Ballets Russes and became one of the public faces of the Return to Order, the classicist swing across French art after the war. The 1920s were, by most accounts, the height of his career: the Carnegie Prize in 1928 for Still-life with Dead Game, exhibitions touring London, Berlin, Frankfurt, Düsseldorf, New York and Cincinnati. Not everyone was convinced the trade had been worth it — the critic Jacques-Émile Blanche dismissed the classicism Derain had settled into as ["highly cerebral and rather mechanical art."](https://theartstory.org/artist/derain-andre/) The painter who had scandalised the Salon d'Automne at twenty-five was, by forty-eight, the thing a younger generation would need to scandalise in turn.

sections.heading: Then, in November 1941, He Went to Berlin
sections.body: Derain was one of several French artists, Maurice de Vlaminck among them, who accepted an invitation from the sculptor Arno Breker — the Third Reich's officially endorsed artist — for a ten-day tour of Germany, framed by Vichy as a cultural exchange that might help free French prisoners of war. It freed no one, and the Nazi press used Derain's presence exactly as intended. After the Liberation he was branded a collaborator and ostracised by former supporters and dealers alike; his own defence, that art stood apart from politics, persuaded almost no one. He died in 1954, hit by a car near Paris. This village, undated by anyone more precise than "c.1912" and unseen in a public exhibition since, has outlasted both the scandal that made Derain famous and the one that nearly erased him — by being forgotten first.
